screens.title: No Connectivity and Physical Checks
screens.narratorSegment: When a device reports no connectivity, the most efficient first step is to check the physical layer. Physical checks include confirming that cables are properly seated, link lights on the NIC and switch port are active, and the correct port is used. These are quick, low‑risk verifications that can rule out obvious causes before you spend time on protocol or server issues. For example, an unplugged patch cable or a failed port will yield no link and no IP assignment. A common misconception is to assume DHCP or DNS is to blame; if the link is down, higher‑level services are unreachable and tests like ping will fail for that reason. An example workflow: verify link lights, swap the cable with a known good one, check port LEDs on both ends, and confirm the NIC is enabled in the OS. If the link is active, proceed to IP configuration checks. Key takeaways are to always start simple, document the physical checks you made, and avoid changing configuration settings until you confirm the link. Ask yourself: did I confirm electrical or optical connectivity before moving to DHCP and IP tests?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › No Connectivity
Definition
Physical Diagnostics

Before running IP tools, rule out cable, port, or NIC failures. Link lights and LED patterns are primary indicators.

  • Check that cables are fully seated and not damaged.
  • Confirm NIC and switch port LEDs show link/activity.
  • Swap with a known‑good cable or port to isolate the fault.
  • Disable and re-enable the NIC in the OS to rule out driver hangs.
Common Mistake
Jumping directly to DHCP or DNS checks without confirming link status.
Practical Example
A laptop with no internet had fading link LEDs because the patch cable was damaged. Replacing the cable restored connectivity and allowed DHCP to assign a proper IP.
Try this checklist
  1. Confirm physical connection and LEDs.
  2. Swap cable and test link again.
  3. Check switch port for errors or disabled state.
  4. If still down, test the NIC on another known-good network segment.
Key Takeaway

Simple physical checks often resolve 'no connectivity' faster than protocol troubleshooting.

screens.title: APIPA and DHCP Failures
screens.narratorSegment: APIPA occurs when a device cannot obtain an IP address from DHCP and assigns itself a 169.254. x. x address. This automatic behavior allows limited local link communications but prevents access to other networks. When you encounter an APIPA address, start by verifying physical connectivity and then check DHCP reachability. On Windows, ipconfig /all reveals the address and the configured DHCP server; a quick ipconfig /release followed by ipconfig /renew forces a new lease request. If renew fails, check DHCP server status, network congestion that may drop DHCP requests, or an incorrectly configured network adapter. A helpful test is to manually set a static address in the correct subnet and then ping the gateway. If that static address reaches the gateway, the issue is likely DHCP. A common misconception is that APIPA means the device is entirely offline; in fact, it may still communicate with other APIPA hosts on the same link. The key is to use methodical tests to distinguish a DHCP server issue from a link problem, and document lease times and server logs where possible. APIPA and DHCP Failures means 169.254.x.x means dhcp didn't respond. renew leases, test static ip, and inspect dhcp server and network path.. In practical terms, identify apipa addresses and restore dhcp leasing. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › APIPA & DHCP
Process
APIPA: quick checks
If an address reads 169.254.x.x, DHCP did not provide a lease. Follow this minimal process to isolate the cause.
  1. Verify link and switch port LEDs.
  2. Run ipconfig /all (or ifconfig) to view IP and DHCP server values.
  3. Attempt ipconfig /release and ipconfig /renew to force DHCP.
  4. If renew fails, test a manual static IP in the subnet and ping gateway.
Command example (Windows)
C:\> ipconfig /release
C:\> ipconfig /renew

# Check results with:
C:\> ipconfig /all
If renew returns a valid IP, DHCP is functioning. If not, inspect DHCP server and network path.
Example Scenario
A user had APIPA; renewing failed. Admin found the DHCP server service had stopped on the router and restarting it restored leases.

screens.title: Default Gateway Problems
screens.narratorSegment: A valid IP address and subnet mask do not guarantee internet access. If a device can communicate locally but cannot reach external networks, the default gateway is the likely suspect. The default gateway is the router's IP that forwards traffic off the local subnet. Use ipconfig or ifconfig to confirm the configured gateway, then ping the gateway's address to test reachability. If ping fails, the fault could be a misconfigured gateway address, a router issue, a bad uplink cable, or a firewall blocking traffic to the gateway. If the gateway is reachable but external addresses are not, traceroute can reveal where packets are dropped outside the local network. A common misconception is that DNS is always the cause of external access failures; sometimes routing or gateway misconfiguration is the root cause. Example: a workstation on 192.168.1.0/24 had a gateway set to 192.168.0.1; local traffic worked but internet did not. Correcting the gateway restored access. Always document the gateway settings before changing them and verify with pings and traceroutes after any fix. Default Gateway Problems means verify the gateway ip and that it responds to ping. if reachable but external access fails, use traceroute to find where traffic stops.. In practical terms, when local ips exist but external networks are unreachable. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Default Gateway
Definition
Gateway Checks and Commands
A reachable gateway is required for traffic leaving the subnet. Verify its IP and reachability before assuming cloud or ISP issues.
Quick checks
  • Confirm gateway IP with ipconfig /all or ifconfig.
  • Ping the gateway: success should be low latency and no packet loss.
  • If ping fails, check router, port, and firewall rules.
Example
A host with gateway configured to a different subnet could not reach the internet. Correcting the gateway IP fixed the routing immediately.
Traceroute use
If gateway responds but external sites do not, run traceroute to see which hop introduces latency or drops traffic. Look for the first external hop showing high delay or timeouts.
Key Takeaway

A misconfigured or unreachable gateway blocks external traffic even when local communication works.

screens.title: Using ping and traceroute
screens.narratorSegment: Ping and traceroute are complementary tools for diagnosing reachability and latency. Ping sends ICMP echo requests to check whether a host responds and to measure round‑trip time and packet loss. Traceroute maps the path packets take through the network and reports the latency at each hop. Use ping first to confirm whether a host is reachable. If ping fails to an external address but the gateway responds, traceroute helps locate the hop where packets stop or delay increases dramatically. For example, if latency jumps at hop three, the device or link at that hop is a likely congestion point. A common confusion is blaming the destination server when multiple intermediate hops show high latency; focus on the first hop that consistently increases delay. Practice example: ping 8.8.8.8 to check reachability and baseline latency, then traceroute to 8.8.8.8 when ping shows high latency to see where the delay occurs. End each test by recording results and repeating tests at different times to capture intermittent issues. Using ping and traceroute means ping confirms reachability; traceroute locates where latency or loss appears. treat the first problematic hop as the focus for investigation.. In practical terms, how to localize latency and reachability issues. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Ping vs Traceroute
Comparison
Ping
Simple reachability and RTT checks. Good for quick verification and packet loss detection.
C:\> ping 8.8.8.8
Pinging 8.8.8.8 with 32 bytes of data:
Reply from 8.8.8.8: bytes=32 time=20ms TTL=117
Interpret: consistent replies with low time indicate good reachability.
Traceroute
Maps each hop so you can see where latency or drops begin. Use after ping shows problems.
C:\> tracert 8.8.8.8
1  192.168.1.1  1 ms
2  203.0.113.1  15 ms
3  198.51.100.2 78 ms
4  8.8.8.8  80 ms
Interpret: latency spike at hop 3 suggests congestion or a slow link there.
Key Takeaway

Use ping to confirm reachability and traceroute to locate where problems begin along the path.

Check your understanding
If ping to 8.8.8.8 fails but gateway ping succeeds, where should you run traceroute first? Answer: from the gateway outward or from the host to identify the next hop showing failure.

screens.title: High Latency and Low Bandwidth
screens.narratorSegment: High latency and low bandwidth are related but distinct performance problems. High latency is a delay in packet round‑trip time and often shows as slow response even when bandwidth appears adequate. Causes include network congestion, overloaded routers or switches, or long physical distance. Low bandwidth reduces transfer rates and creates slow file transfers or buffering; common causes include duplex mismatches, faulty cables, outdated drivers, or an overloaded internet connection. To diagnose latency, use ping and traceroute to find where delays occur; repeated tests during peak and off‑peak hours reveal intermittent congestion. For low throughput, check duplex settings on both NIC and switch, verify cables, and update drivers. A duplex mismatch — one side set to full and the other to half — causes packet collisions and severe speed reduction. A common misconception is treating latency as bandwidth; a connection with low latency can still be bandwidth‑constrained. Always capture baseline metrics so you can compare before and after any change. High Latency and Low Bandwidth means ping/traceroute find latency; interface checks and cable inspection find throughput issues. duplex mismatch often looks like slow transfers with low local ping.. In practical terms, different symptoms, different causes, related detection steps. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Latency & Bandwidth
Comparison
High Latency
Symptoms: slow response times, laggy applications. Tools: ping and traceroute to locate hops with increased delay.
  • Look for consistent delay spikes at a particular hop.
  • Test at different times to detect congestion.
  • Consider physical distance as a natural source of latency.
Low Bandwidth
Symptoms: slow file transfers or streaming despite low ping. Tools: check NIC and switch duplex, test transfer rates, inspect cables and drivers.
  • Verify speed & duplex settings on both ends; prefer Auto Negotiation.
  • Replace suspect cables and update drivers.
  • Test with a known-good server on the LAN to isolate ISP vs local issues.
Key Takeaway

Measure both latency and throughput. Duplex mismatches often cause low bandwidth with acceptable ping to local devices.

Pro tip
When in doubt, test transfers across a local server to rule out ISP or external issues.

screens.title: Duplex Mismatch
screens.narratorSegment: A duplex mismatch happens when two connected devices use different duplex settings — one set to full‑duplex and the other to half‑duplex. Full‑duplex allows simultaneous send and receive, while half‑duplex forces devices to share the medium, leading to collisions and retransmissions. The result is severe throughput degradation and often asymmetrical performance. You might see good ping results to local hosts but very slow transfer speeds. To verify duplex mismatch, check the NIC settings in the OS and the switch port settings. Modern best practice is Auto Negotiation on both ends so they agree on the highest supported speed and duplex. If Auto Negotiation is disabled on one side, manually set the other side to match. A common troubleshooting sequence: check link speed and duplex on both ends, set both to Auto, replace cables if problems persist, and update network drivers. Remember to document any manual changes and test file transfers to confirm improvement. Duplex Mismatch means use auto negotiation or ensure both ends match. a mismatch causes collisions and poor throughput even when simple pings succeed.. In practical terms, how different duplex settings degrade throughput. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Duplex Mismatch
Definition & Fix
What is duplex mismatch?
A mismatch between full and half duplex causes collisions, retransmissions, and low throughput despite successful pings.

screens.title: DNS Resolution Failures
screens.narratorSegment: DNS failures are a common cause of apparent connectivity problems: you can ping an IP address but not a hostname. Start by confirming you can reach the DNS server's IP with ping. Then use nslookup to query a known public server such as 8.8.8.8 and compare that to a query using the configured DNS server. If nslookup succeeds with a public DNS server but fails with the local DNS server, the local DNS is the issue — check its configuration and logs. If the configured DNS server is unreachable by ping, you have a reachability problem, not DNS. Typical causes include wrong DNS addresses on the client, a failing DNS service, or a firewall blocking UDP port 53. Example commands: run ipconfig /all to see configured DNS servers, then nslookup google. com 8.8.8.8 to test a known resolver. Keep in mind that caching and propagation can lead to intermittent name resolution problems, so repeat tests and document results to spot patterns. screens.title: Intermittent Issues and Systematic Troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: Intermittent faults are the hardest to fix because they do not present consistently. The right approach is systematic: reproduce the problem if possible, enable detailed logging, monitor at different times, and try to isolate variables. Start by gathering detailed symptoms: exact times, user actions, and any correlated events like backups or scheduled tasks. Use continuous ping or scripted traceroutes to capture when failures occur; collect AP or router logs for association and error events. When you can reproduce the issue, change one parameter at a time — for example, swap cables, change AP channels, or temporarily move the user to a different AP — and observe whether the problem follows the change. Keep careful documentation of each change and its effect. Common pitfalls are changing multiple settings at once and not allowing enough time after a change to verify stability. If hardware is suspected, schedule a planned replacement or swap for testing during low-impact hours. Patience and disciplined logging are your best tools for intermittent network problems. In this chapter you will learn to recognize the common symptoms of networking problems and apply reliable fixes. We'll start with the basics: how physical faults or a missing DHCP lease lead to no connectivity, and move through diagnosing default gateway problems, latency and bandwidth bottlenecks, DNS failures, and Wi‑Fi signal and interference issues. Each topic pairs simple commands and observations with hands‑on checks you can perform quickly in the field. For example, seeing a 169.254. x. x address tells you the device failed to receive a DHCP lease, which focuses your next step on DHCP server health or connectivity. You will also practice forming a hypothesis, testing it with tools like ping, traceroute, and nslookup, and then verifying the fix. Along the way we'll highlight common mistakes, such as assuming a site is down when DNS is the culprit, or overlooking duplex mismatches that throttle throughput. By the end, you'll have a compact, repeatable troubleshooting workflow for both steady failures and intermittent issues. Think about a recent connectivity problem you faced: which first check would you run to narrow the cause?

These objectives map to the practical skills you'll practice in this chapter. First, you will learn to diagnose and resolve basic connectivity problems, including recognizing APIPA addresses and using lease renewal commands. That skill matters because the wrong first step wastes time — checking DHCP and link lights quickly narrows the scope. Second, you'll troubleshoot performance issues: identify high latency with ping and traceroute, and diagnose low bandwidth by checking duplex settings, cables, and drivers. Third, you'll identify and correct DNS resolution failures by verifying DNS server configuration, using nslookup, and isolating whether DNS or connectivity is the root cause. Finally, you will address Wi‑Fi connectivity and signal strength problems by measuring signal levels, checking channel interference, and validating SSID and security settings. Each objective includes a quick mnemonic or simple visual to help you remember the ordered troubleshooting steps. Complete all four to reach the verified competency milestone for basic network troubleshooting.

This objective slide focuses on the tools and the systematic process you'll use repeatedly. The process is simple: gather information, form a hypothesis, test the hypothesis with targeted tools, implement a fix, and verify the outcome. You'll rely on OS and network commands such as ipconfig or ifconfig for IP state, ping to check reachability and basic packet loss, traceroute to find where latency spikes occur, and nslookup to validate DNS resolution. For Windows troubleshooting you will practice ipconfig release and renew to force DHCP interactions. For Wi‑Fi, you'll learn to use built‑in signal meters or lightweight analyzers to detect weak signal or interference. Always document the steps you take so intermittent problems, which often reappear under load or specific conditions, can be reproduced. Avoid common mistakes: don't change multiple settings at once, and don't assume the first symptom is the root cause. With disciplined steps and these tools, you can systematically isolate and solve the majority of network issues.

When a device reports no connectivity, the most efficient first step is to check the physical layer. Physical checks include confirming that cables are properly seated, link lights on the NIC and switch port are active, and the correct port is used. These are quick, low‑risk verifications that can rule out obvious causes before you spend time on protocol or server issues. For example, an unplugged patch cable or a failed port will yield no link and no IP assignment. A common misconception is to assume DHCP or DNS is to blame; if the link is down, higher‑level services are unreachable and tests like ping will fail for that reason. An example workflow: verify link lights, swap the cable with a known good one, check port LEDs on both ends, and confirm the NIC is enabled in the OS. If the link is active, proceed to IP configuration checks. Key takeaways are to always start simple, document the physical checks you made, and avoid changing configuration settings until you confirm the link. Ask yourself: did I confirm electrical or optical connectivity before moving to DHCP and IP tests?

APIPA occurs when a device cannot obtain an IP address from DHCP and assigns itself a 169.254. x. x address. This automatic behavior allows limited local link communications but prevents access to other networks. When you encounter an APIPA address, start by verifying physical connectivity and then check DHCP reachability. On Windows, ipconfig /all reveals the address and the configured DHCP server; a quick ipconfig /release followed by ipconfig /renew forces a new lease request. If renew fails, check DHCP server status, network congestion that may drop DHCP requests, or an incorrectly configured network adapter. A helpful test is to manually set a static address in the correct subnet and then ping the gateway. If that static address reaches the gateway, the issue is likely DHCP. A common misconception is that APIPA means the device is entirely offline; in fact, it may still communicate with other APIPA hosts on the same link. The key is to use methodical tests to distinguish a DHCP server issue from a link problem, and document lease times and server logs where possible. A valid IP address and subnet mask do not guarantee internet access. If a device can communicate locally but cannot reach external networks, the default gateway is the likely suspect. The default gateway is the router's IP that forwards traffic off the local subnet. Use ipconfig or ifconfig to confirm the configured gateway, then ping the gateway's address to test reachability. If ping fails, the fault could be a misconfigured gateway address, a router issue, a bad uplink cable, or a firewall blocking traffic to the gateway.
